accuracy.evidence: Presents the trigger, feeling, action sequence the way KS1 PSHE and CASEL self-awareness frame it: an event happens, a feeling follows, behaviour comes after. The 'look back' idea (a cause from earlier in the day) and the role of tiredness and hunger in making feelings bigger are consistent with research on sleep loss and emotional reactivity in young children and on hunger shaping emotion (MacCormack and Lindquist). The adult text states clearly that a trigger explains a feeling but does not excuse hurting anyone.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors 5 to 7 year olds actually make: naming the feeling as its own cause ('sad because I was sad', challenge tag feel), giving the action that came after ('because I cried', tag act), blaming whatever is nearest in time (the comic look-back step where Leo's cause is in panel 1, not lunch), believing feelings come from nowhere (tag nowhere) and picking a cause that does not fit the feeling (tag odd).

lab_distinct.evidence: flag_cause.js is about causes of feelings, not naming or regulating them: drag-a-happening onto three children's faces, a happened-or-feeling sort of six cards, a three-panel comic to scan back for an earlier trigger, sleep and tummy meters for body causes, and an 'I feel ... when ...' sentence builder. It passed the 30% shingle gate against every other flag lab, including the existing feelings-naming and calming labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each task practises one part of the topic: matching three happenings to Mia, Leo and Ava rehearses 'felt X because Y'; the sort separates trigger from feeling; the comic makes the child look before the moment of the feeling; the meters show that tired and hungry make a small thing feel big; the builder has the child name two of their own triggers with different feelings, as the topic statement asks.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong answers children really give: 'My brother took my toy' asked as a feeling (many say yes), 'What made Leo grumpy at lunch?' where the lunch itself is the tempting near-in-time pick, and whether being tired can make a twisted sock feel bigger. Each is then tested on the canvas and the reveal states the reason.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Rotating questions such as 'Sam felt scared. What was the trigger?' with every wrong choice tagged (feel, act, nowhere, odd) and a specific message, e.g. 'That is the feeling, not the cause. Ask: what happened first?' and 'That is what they did after the feeling. The trigger came before.' Choice order rotates each round.

readability.evidence: Family audience: kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (sad, cross, tired, hungry) and pass the FK 5.0 target; adult paragraphs pass the 10.0 target and give scope, the three key ideas, named mistakes and a lab tour. Canvas cards pair each feeling word with a face emoji so a grown-up can read along with a pre-reader.

no_filler.evidence: No filler phrases (gate passed). Every kid sentence is an example or a rule (something happens first, the trigger is not the feeling, look back, tired and hungry make feelings bigger). Hints say exactly what to ask, for instance 'Ask: what happened first?', rather than general encouragement.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 (390 px) screenshots in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: the three happening cards and three child faces fit in one row each, the six sort cards stack into two labelled bins without clipping, the comic panels and meters are full-width, and the sentence builder's four feeling tiles and six happening tiles are big tap targets.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a button twin (child buttons for matching, What happened / Feeling bin buttons, Picture 1 to 3, Check sleep, Check tummy); the canvas aria-label updates with each message and a polite live region announces feedback. Correct answers are stated in words, not colour alone. axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in light or dark on every step, before and after Show me.
